scenarioName: Aortic Dissection — Sudden Tearing Chest Pain at the Bank, Bilateral BP Differential, ASA Withheld, Load-and-Go

scenarioStory.history: 58-year-old male was sitting at his desk typing when he was struck — with zero warning — by the worst pain of his life. Onset was instantaneous and abrupt: 'I was just sitting here, and BAM!' The quality is NOT pressure — he is emphatic that it is a tearing, ripping feeling unlike anything he has ever felt. It started in the middle of his chest and goes straight through to his back, right between the shoulder blades. Nothing he does makes it better; it hurts to even breathe. Severity is 10/10 — 'the absolute worst.' It started about 5 minutes before his coworker called 911 and has not changed at all since onset. His only medical history is hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril — but he ran out several days ago and has not taken it since. He is pale, sweating profusely, restless, and unable to find a comfortable position.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: EMS finds a 58-year-old man in agonizing distress with the classic dissection story told almost word for word: instantaneous onset while at rest, a TEARING/RIPPING quality he insists is not pressure, radiation from mid-chest straight through to the interscapular back, 10/10 and unchanged, in a hypertensive patient who stopped his lisinopril days ago. He is A&Ox4, patent airway, breathing fast but not labored, with bounding rapid pulses and pale, cool, clammy skin. The crew's exam is where this case is won or lost: blood pressure obtained in BOTH arms reveals 198/110 on the right versus 150/90 on the left — a 48 mmHg systolic differential — and the left radial pulse is palpably weaker than the bounding right. Under MATC guidance this presentation maps to the Back Pain guideline's life-threat screen for aortic dissection (chest pain with back pain, unequal pulses/perfusion) and to the ACS guideline's deferral clause for likely non-cardiac chest pain: aspirin and nitrates are withheld and pain is managed per the Pain Management guideline — at this crew's BLS scope, position of comfort and verbal reassurance, not analgesics. Definitive care is surgical — the correct posture is recognition, minimal scene time, and transport toward an appropriate facility with a specialty destination considered. Every additional minute on scene is myocardium-irrelevant and aorta-critical. → ASA held; load-and-go: The crew got the two decisions that matter right: no aspirin, no lingering. The patient is moved to the stretcher quickly but carefully, kept sitting up in his position of comfort, and wheeled straight through the lobby to the ambulance. What the crew still owes him under MATC at BLS scope is compassionate, non-pharmacologic pain care: position of comfort and verbal reassurance are named options in the Pain Management guideline, and a documented NRS baseline — 10/10 — starts the trend line the receiving team will need. As he settles onto the stretcher, stiller and coached through his breathing, the catecholamine surge eases fractionally and his pressure begins to drift down from its 198 systolic peak on the right. Early notification lets the receiving facility start assembling what this man actually needs — imaging and a surgical decision — before the ambulance is on the ramp. → Packaged; en route: En route, non-pharmacologic care does what it can: sitting up in his position of comfort, coached breathing, and steady reassurance leave him calmer and stiller, and with the sympathetic surge fractionally blunted his right-arm pressure drifts down from 198 to 172 systolic. His pain remains severe — 9/10 — and the differential persists; it is a structural finding, and nothing in a BLS bag fixes it. The crew's job now is disciplined reassessment: vitals and response to interventions throughout transport, serial NRS pain scores recorded with repeat vitals, and eyes on him for any sign of deterioration — sudden pain change, syncope, signs of shock. Documentation closes the loop: symptom-onset time and — the line item this scenario exists to teach — the reason aspirin was NOT given. Per the source presentation, his condition remains critical but does not deteriorate during transport: the crew gave him the best possible chance by recognizing the emergency and moving.

scenarioEvents.name: ASA given; scene prolonged
scenarioEvents.description: The crew read 'chest pain' and ran the ACS play from memory: a long on-scene secondary assessment, non-pertinent questions, no second-arm blood pressure — and 324 mg of chewed aspirin. Shortly after the aspirin goes in, the patient lets out a cry; his pain suddenly worsens and he goes much more pale. Scene time is past 10 minutes and the physiology is now moving: heart rate climbing through the 130s, right-arm systolic FALLING from 198 to 158 — a falling pressure in a hypertensive dissection patient is not improvement, it is leaking — and the left radial is now barely palpable. He says the words that should ice every spine in the room: 'I feel very dizzy...' This phase is the last exit. What MATC still offers at BLS scope: recognize the deterioration for what it is, assess for shock per the Back Pain guideline, get the AED pads on a patient who is about to arrest, and move NOW — abandon everything on scene that is not the stretcher. What no protocol offers: a way to take the aspirin back.
relatedChecklist: Recognize deterioration — sudden pain change, pallor, dizziness = evolving catastrophe
Assess for shock — falling BP, climbing HR, cold gray skin after sudden pain change
AED pads ON now — this patient is peri-arrest
Abort on-scene care; move NOW — appropriate facility, notify en route

scenarioEvents.name: Rupture — cardiac arrest
scenarioEvents.description: His eyes roll back mid-sentence and he slumps in the chair. No carotid pulse. Blood pressure unobtainable. A few agonal gasps, then apnea. The AED goes on and analyzes: NO SHOCK ADVISED — organized complexes are marching along at 40 with no pulse: PEA, the rhythm of an empty heart. The aorta has completely ruptured; the delay on scene has produced the outcome the load-and-go pathway exists to prevent. The crew now runs the MATC Cardiac Arrest guideline at BLS scope with full understanding of what it can and cannot buy: immediate, minimally interrupted high-quality compressions with rescuers rotating before fatigue; the 2-minute cycle of compressions and rhythm analysis, with compressions continuing through AED analysis-to-charge gaps; an OPA and BVM ventilation delivered so that nothing about the airway interrupts compressions; and resuscitation where he lies, not in a moving ambulance. Debrief honestly: the arrest was not caused by the failure to resuscitate well — it was caused by the aspirin and the ten minutes.
relatedChecklist: Immediate high-quality compressions — 100–120/min, 2–2.4 inches, full recoil, rotate q2min
Witnessed arrest: AED on, analyze immediately — no shock advised; 2-minute cycles
Airway without stopping compressions — OPA + BVM 30:2 or 10/min on the upstroke
Work the arrest where he lies — no compressions in a moving ambulance
